column1: Time-Varying Identification of Monetary Policy Shocks

The thesis titled Time-Varying Identification of Monetary Policy Shocks by Annika Camehl and Tomasz Woźniak introduces a novel approach to understanding monetary policy shocks in the United States. The authors propose a Bayesian heteroskedastic Markov-switching structural vector autoregression (SVAR) model with time-varying identification (TVI) to analyze these shocks. This model allows for the selection of alternative exclusion restrictions within different regimes and verifies identification through heteroskedasticity. The study finds that US data supports time variation in the identification of monetary policy shocks.

The research identifies two main regimes in US monetary policy. The first regime  which dominates the sample period  follows a Taylor rule extended by the term spread  effectively controlling inflation. The second regime  which gains persistence after the global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic  is characterized by a money-augmented Taylor rule that provides economic stimulus and features the liquidity effect.

The authors argue that the Federal Reserve's targeting strategy has evolved significantly over the past sixty years  moving from money supply adjustments to inflation-targeting interest rate policies. Despite these changes  traditional empirical studies often assume time-invariant identification of monetary policy shocks  which may not align with reality. The authors address this by implementing a time-varying identification strategy using a data-driven search mechanism.

The proposed model  a Bayesian Markov-switching SVAR with TVI and heteroskedasticity  automatically selects exclusion restrictions to identify monetary policy shocks within each regime. A new prior distribution is introduced to estimate a TVI indicator  allowing structural parameters to vary across regimes. This approach does not assume a specific identifying pattern for each regime  instead letting the data determine the supported exclusion restrictions.

The model's regime-dependent selection of exclusion restrictions is validated through identification via heteroskedasticity. The structural matrix follows a slow-moving Markov-switching process  while the structural shocks' variances evolve at a higher frequency according to a stochastic volatility process. This setup enables the identification of shocks via heteroskedasticity within a regime  making the exclusion restrictions overidentifying and allowing for discrimination among them in the data-driven search.

The study uses six US monthly time series from January 1960 to June 2023  including industrial production  consumer price index inflation  federal funds rate  term spread  M3 money  and stock prices. The authors find strong evidence of time variation in US monetary policy shock identification. In the first regime  data supports including term spreads in the Taylor Rule  suggesting that conventional monetary policy considers the bond yield curve's slope. In the second regime  data supports a monetary policy rule augmented by the monetary aggregate  providing substantial economic stimulus and steepening the bond yield curve.

The results indicate that monetary policy in the second regime cushioned the economy after crises  boosting activity with a slight increase in inflation. The study concludes that time-varying identification sharpens the understanding of monetary policy shocks and their effects  providing a more nuanced view of the Federal Reserve's policy evolution and its impact on the economy.
